text: Imitation learning is limited in spatial generalization and in multi-stage tasks. Traditional task and motion planning, or TAMP, is often brittle in contact-rich operations. So, can we complement the strengths of both? We propose DR-LfD. It decomposes demonstrations into reusable skills, and a planner reorganizes them to solve new tasks.

Let me show you an example. DR-LfD can achieve user-specified goals that mix learned skills, like object handoff, with planned skills, like dropping an object into a basket. On the left is the only operation we demonstrated: handing off a tape. On the right, the instruction is: all tapes to the basket. The planner reuses the handoff for every tape, and adds the drops by itself.

DR-LfD also scales to long-horizon tasks. On the left are three skills, each demonstrated separately: screwdriver packing, cup handoff, and cup wiping. Now we give a new instruction: complete the cup wiping and screwdriver packing tasks, and leave all objects on the table. The planner chains the skills into one plan: hand off the cup, wipe it, put down the sponge and cup, then pack the screwdriver. That is nineteen steps in total.
Because a planner is in the loop, the robot also respects physical constraints: reachability on the left, and safety on the right.

Now, why not just use imitation learning? The problem is spatial generalization. The diversity of demonstration data is limited by both the workspace of the teleoperation hardware and the kinematics of the human operator. You can see that diffusion policy works at the demonstrated placement, but fails at all four new ones.
In general, visuomotor imitation policies, like diffusion policy, are often brittle under unseen object placements.
And we cannot simply collect more data. For some placements, like the one on the right, the operator fails to perform the teleoperation at all.
Next, let's go through our experiment recordings. This table lists the tasks, the robots, and the four test setups.
We start with screwdriver packing on a dual-arm Franka robot. Here is a demonstration.
In the OOD setup, we place the screwdriver at random headings and positions outside the training data. As you can see, the robot still grasps it and packs it into the box.
Next is the same task on the ALOHA robot. Again, a demonstration first.
Under OOD placements, DR-LfD keeps packing the screwdriver reliably, while diffusion policy mostly fails.
In the Leaky setup, the screwdriver leans on another object, so the robot has to grasp it from a tilted pose.
The next task is object handoff on ALOHA.
The right arm picks up the tape and passes it to the left arm. Again, from new placements, DR-LfD stays reliable, while diffusion policy mostly fails.
It also works in the Leaky setup, where the tape leans against a support.
Next, cup-sleeve insertion.
This task needs a fine insertion. With tilted cups and sleeves, it stays hard for every method, including ours.
We also test peg-in-hole insertion in simulation, using the scripted dataset from Zhao et al.
From OOD placements, the robot grasps the peg and the socket, and then runs the learned insertion skill.

What if an object is out of reach? In the Unreachable setup, the socket starts beyond the left arm's workspace. So the right arm first moves it to the middle of the table, where the left arm can grasp it. This extra step was never demonstrated, and the imitation baselines fail in all such cases.

What if an obstacle is in the way? In the Unsafe setup, a pole blocks the insertion and may cause a collision. The planner first moves the pole aside, and then inserts. Again, it is the planner that adds this step, not the demonstrations.
Back on ALOHA, here is the long cup, sponge, and screwdriver task. Even from new placements, DR-LfD can still succeed, while diffusion policy never does.

DR-LfD is also robust in closed loop. A contact detector locates failed subgoals and triggers replanning. Here, a person moves the screwdriver, the cup, and the sponge, and the robot replans each time.
We also ran stress tests. With new objects, the main bottleneck lies in the low-level visuomotor policy.
The good news is that we can fix this by strengthening the weak skills. Two skills failed in the cluttered background. Five more demonstrations per skill fix this distribution shift.
Finally, here are typical failures of DR-LfD: unexpected dynamics,
inaccurate grasps,
policy failures,
and, hardware failures.
